headline: Android's built-in webcam mode instantly improves video call quality
summary: Android 14's native USB webcam mode offers plug-and-play functionality and superior video quality compared to many dedicated webcams, with no extra software needed.
details: Tired of grainy, poorly lit video calls? Android's built-in webcam mode, introduced with Android 14, offers a surprisingly effective solution. By simply connecting your phone to your computer via USB, you can instantly upgrade your video conferencing experience.

The native webcam mode is easy to set up: connect your phone, tap the USB notification, and select 'Webcam'. Your phone then acts as a standard USB Video Class (UVC) device, compatible with Windows, Linux, and Chrome OS without requiring any drivers or third-party software.

In testing, the author found that their Android phone's camera significantly outperformed their desktop's dedicated webcam, especially in artificial lighting. This is largely due to the superior sensors found in modern smartphones, even budget models, compared to the often-outdated hardware in many webcams.

Beyond basic functionality, Android's webcam mode allows switching between front and back cameras, including ultrawide and telephoto lenses. It also forwards audio from the phone's microphone, providing a comprehensive audio-visual solution.

While dedicated webcams have seen little innovation over the past decade, smartphone cameras have advanced considerably. Achieving comparable quality with a traditional webcam often requires spending over $100, making the built-in Android feature a compelling alternative.

A key feature missing from Android's native mode is wireless connectivity, a feature Apple offers with its Continuity Camera. While third-party apps like DroidCam can provide wireless functionality, they require additional software installation on the computer.

headline_marked: Solar panel breakthrough could [[nearly double]] efficiency to 43%
headline: Solar panel breakthrough could nearly double efficiency to 43%
summary: Researchers have developed a new solar panel design that addresses energy loss, potentially pushing efficiency past current theoretical limits.
details: Researchers at the Institut de Ciències Fotòniques (ICFO) have discovered a novel way to design solar panels that can dramatically increase their energy efficiency. While existing studies have focused on reducing heat loss, ICFO's research addresses Boltzmann loss, the energy lost to the light solar panels emit.

This new approach could theoretically boost panel efficiency from the current theoretical limit of 33.16 percent (the Shockley-Queisser limit) to approximately 43 percent. This is a significant leap from typical consumer solar panels, which perform at 20 to 23 percent efficiency.

The ICFO team addressed the mismatch between the narrow sunlight absorption and the wider emission cones of solar panels. They achieved this by replacing the indium tin oxide front electrode with a thin silver one and converting the organic solar cell into an optical cavity.

This modification created a cell that still allowed sunlight in but emitted less light at wide angles, improving its efficiency by around 0.85 percent. This modest gain provides evidence that solar cell efficiency can be pushed beyond the theoretical limit.

Dr. Francisco Bernal Texca, the study's first author, stated that if the emission cone can be narrowed to match the absorption cone of incoming sunlight, solar cells could approach efficiencies close to 43 percent. The underlying principle is expected to apply to all types of photovoltaic cells.
